frameworks.name: Four Wealth Acquisition Groups
frameworks.definition: A typology distinguishing how different groups use money and time: the rich buy time, the poor buy stuff, ambitious people buy skills, lazy people buy distractions.

frameworks.name: Generational Wealth Transfer Through Skills
frameworks.definition: Wealth compounds across generations only when transferred as skills and education, not as accumulated assets; a son without skills renders inherited wealth irrelevant.

frameworks.name: Focus as Constraint
frameworks.definition: Focus is operationally measurable by the count of things you say no to; maximum focus is saying yes to one thing and saying no to everything else.

claims.text: Ambition is not the same as action. Ambitious people can remain poor when they are distracted—splitting effort across many income streams instead of focusing on one. The belief that multiple income streams create wealth is false; seven income streams spread effort seven ways, making the person work harder but not richer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to founders with founder-dependent business models
where the founder is required to rainmake across multiple business lines
claims.mechanism: Splitting effort dilutes the founder's capacity to reach escape velocity on any single business; income streams do not scale without founder leverage.

anchors.value: founder still required to rainmake across all, business remains stuck

bounded_by: Does not apply to passive asset portfolios where owner is not required to personally execute
Does not apply after founder has achieved genuine business leverage

claims.text: Generational wealth transfer through assets alone fails. The Sanskrit proverb captures this: 'If you have a good son, you don't need to accumulate wealth; if you have a bad son, there's no point in accumulating wealth.' Wealth is inherited through skills, not stuff.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: where the heir's skill level determines wealth's utility
claims.mechanism: A son with skills will compound inherited capital; a son without skills will squander it regardless of initial transfer size. Skills are the binding constraint on generational wealth utility.
bounded_by: Does not apply to trust structures designed to remove discretion from the heir

claims.text: Lazy people avoid self-confrontation by consuming feel-good distraction content (entertainment, motivational messaging that affirms worthiness) rather than accepting the painful reality that they are inadequate. This pattern perpetuates poverty.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: describes a psychological pattern in wealth-building
applies to people choosing avoidance over skill investment
claims.mechanism: Confronting inadequacy is painful; distractions provide emotional relief and false confidence ('I am worthy, I deserve these things'). The pattern prevents the person from investing in skill building, which is the path to wealth creation.
bounded_by: Does not apply to people actively investing time in skill acquisition

claims.text: Entitlement destroys gratitude, which itself is a primary driver of subjective well-being. When you feel entitled to something and receive it, you cannot be grateful because you believe you deserved it. Gratitude requires expecting nothing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to the psychological relationship between expectations and satisfaction
claims.mechanism: Entitlement (expectation of deserving) prevents the mindset of gratitude (expectation of nothing). Gratitude increases life satisfaction; entitlement blocks gratitude. Therefore entitlement reduces subjective well-being.
bounded_by: Is a psychological mechanism, not a universal law; individual variance in how gratitude and entitlement correlate with well-being may exist

claims.text: Your worth is currently equal to what you have already earned. You are worthy of minimum-wage compensation because you have already proven you can work a minimum-wage job. Worthiness is not about identity or inherent value; it is about demonstrated capability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: describes how to operationalize self-worth in economic terms
claims.mechanism: Decoupling self-worth from inherent identity and grounding it in demonstrated economic output removes the entitlement psychology and creates a clear feedback loop: improve output → improve worthiness. This framework prevents the shame spiral that blocks skill investment.
bounded_by: Does not apply to moral or ethical worth
Does not apply to situations where the person lacks agency to improve output

claims.text: To scale a business beyond the founder's personal capacity, the founder must stop being the person required to rainmake (sales) or deliver. Founder-dependent businesses are capped at the founder's personal output limits.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to service businesses and skill-dependent operations
where the founder is the primary revenue-generation or delivery mechanism
claims.mechanism: If the founder is required to work inside the business (rainmake, deliver), the business's output ceiling is the founder's personal capacity. Removing the founder from critical path (hiring salespeople, productizing delivery) is the only path to scale.
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses that have already achieved leverage
Does not apply to founders who have hired replacements and exited personal-touch revenue roles

claims.text: Focus is operationally defined by the number of things you say no to. Maximum focus is saying yes to exactly one thing and saying no to everything else. Inversely, the least focused person says yes to many things.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: describes how to measure focus as a business discipline
claims.mechanism: Each yes removes cognitive and time bandwidth from other pursuits. Saying no is the only way to concentrate effort. The number of 'nos' is proportional to depth of focus.

numbers.axis: focus as a function of rejection rate

bounded_by: Does not prescribe which one thing to focus on
Does not account for portfolio strategies where diversification is intentional leverage

examples.text: Alex Hormozi ran nine separate businesses at his peak: a chiropractor agency, a dental agency, a gym turnaround business with six locations, and several others. He still had to personally rainmake (sell customers) for all nine despite having partners in each business. The result was founder dependency across all nine businesses simultaneously. He was not building wealth faster than someone running one business well; he was spreading his effort so thin that no single business could reach escape velocity.

A person working a minimum-wage job has demonstrated sufficient capability to earn that wage rate. Their worth, in economic terms, is therefore minimum wage. Improving that worth requires demonstrating improved capability: a more skilled job, faster output, or higher-value delivery. The framework decouples moral worth from economic worth and creates a clear, actionable feedback loop.

practices.text: If you are a business owner not growing as fast as you'd like, use the acquisition.com $100M scaling roadmap. Plug in your business information to identify what stage of growth you are at and what the most important priorities are for your specific functions (product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, human resources, finance).

Stop consuming entertainment and distraction content. Instead, invest time in skill acquisition—reading, courses, deliberate practice—even when that investment feels uncomfortable or when you feel inadequate. This is the only path to breaking the lazy-person distraction loop.

Measure your focus operationally: count how many things you say no to this week. If the count is low, you are scattered. Increase your focus by actively saying no to more opportunities, distractions, and secondary business ideas.
